comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C35-C45, C100-C102 regarding electrophysiological evidence for spike-frequency adaptation and GIRK currents. Both evaluations find the evidence SUPPORTED with no methodological concerns. Reviewers describe the work as 'well-executed' and 'rigorous.'

Strong agreement on Ca2+-dependent rundown and barbadin experiments (C47-C54, C108-C111). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers specifically praise the barbadin approach as 'technically precise and mechanistically informative.' OpenEval R2 addresses 10 claims while peer R2 addresses 18 claims (including C112-C119 from OpenEval R3).

Both address control experiments with atipamezole and tertiapin-Q (C112-C119). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED for dissecting receptor vs. channel involvement. Peer review also finds this SUPPORTED as part of their broader evaluation of the barbadin/internalization experiments.

Disagreement on immunohistochemistry and Western blot evidence for receptor internalization (C57-C58, C120-C125). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED with appropriate methods. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to concerns about potential labeling errors in Figure S7 where α2A-AR and TH signals appear similar, recommending re-examination of raw data.

Agreement on dose-response relationship between stress duration and GIRK-I amplitude (C6, C126-C131). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate statistical comparisons and adequate sample sizes. Peer reviewers describe evidence for LC overexcitation as 'compelling.'

Agreement on qPCR data characterizing receptor and channel expression (C83-C86). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes modest sample sizes but appropriate methods. Peer reviewers praise the integration of multiple methodologies including mRNA quantification.

Disagreement on MAO-A upregulation evidence (C10, C87, C89-C91). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED based on Western blot data. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, stating 'concerns regarding the lack of rigor in differential MAO-A expression in fluorescence imaging were not addressed experimentally' and requesting enzymatic assay or quantitative reanalysis.

Agreement on AEP measurements (C11, C88, C92). Both find evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate quantitative validation. Peer reviewers identify MAO-A-DOPEGAL-AEP pathway involvement as a strength, with no specific concerns about AEP measurements.

Disagreement on tau pathology findings (C12, C93-C95). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate quantitative validation. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, raising critical concern that 'AEP-mediated tau cleavage in wild-type mice is minimal and generally insufficient to cause significant behavioral alterations,' questioning physiological relevance.

Strong disagreement on behavioral evidence (C71, C96). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED despite noting missing anxiety figure. Peer review rates UNSUPPORTED, stating 'behavioral analysis remains insufficient to support claims of cognitive impairment' and that 'use of a single working memory test following an anxiety test is inadequate.'

Agreement on mechanistic model limitations (C13, C60, C62-C64, C66, C82, C97-C99). Both rate UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes lack of direct cytosolic NA measurement. Peer review emphasizes 'no direct measurement of cytosolic NA levels or MAO-A enzymatic activity' and that manuscript 'reads as a sequence of discrete experiments rather than a single causal chain.'

Agreement on age validation experiments (C75-C77). Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate validation in adult mice. Peer reviewers raise no concerns about this control, though note lack of sex difference investigation.

Disagreement on overall mechanistic model (C80-C81, C103). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with coherent integration of data, though acknowledging some inferential links. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, stating the study 'falls short in providing the experimental rigor necessary to establish causality' and relies on 'indirect reasoning.'

Disagreement on therapeutic implications (C14, C73). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting claims are speculative without proof-of-concept experiments. Peer review finds SUPPORTED, consistently noting 'translational relevance' and therapeutic strategies as a strength.
